5loqe3njr3d08matfvptk7pnqg.value: Credits: the spacetime algebra, with boosts as rotors, the spacetime split into relative vectors σₖ = γₖγ₀, the field as one bivector F = E + IB and a charge's motion as u turned by e^(dτF/2), is David Hestenes' (Space-Time Algebra, 1966; New Foundations for Classical Mechanics, 1986), as presented by Chris Doran and Anthony Lasenby (Geometric Algebra for Physicists, 2003) (prior art). Relativistic velocity addition is Einstein's (1905), rapidity as the quantity that adds is Robb's (1911), the force on a charge is Lorentz's, and the transformed fields are Lorentz's and Einstein's (prior art); here they come out of the rotor product rather than being written in. The train and the ball are the usual way to tell it (influence). The page, its pictures and its words are ours.

a77garobvg4r03jho0j9bkubja.value: Two questions about things that move very fast, each answered first the everyday way, Newton's, and then the way this program does it. The page is a program in our language. All of its physics is one piece of algebra, the spacetime algebra, but you don't need any symbols to follow along. They are kept for a box at the very end.

8fr8rfuoqahou12fqi6dm9cl5u.value: Picture a train going along a platform. Someone on the train throws a ball forwards. We know how fast the train goes, and how fast the ball leaves the thrower's hand, measured by people on the train. How fast does someone standing on the platform see the ball go?

40bq9icmhv2l5haprebtn6hhb8.value: Newton's answer is: add them. A train at 100 km/h and a ball thrown at 30 km/h make a ball going at 130 km/h for the platform. For trains and balls this is right, as closely as anyone can measure.

id6kndidi3hvjr4473od777kj7.value: From here on, speeds are measured against the speed of light: 1 means as fast as light, 0.5 means half as fast. Light goes about 300,000 km a second, so even 0.01 is very fast, and a real train is at about 0.0000001.

4bfktkkg279v25tb8b6e563ufd.value: Now make the train go at 0.6 and throw the ball at 0.6. Newton says 1.2, faster than light. But nothing has ever been measured going faster than light, and experiments with fast particles agree with Einstein's answer from 1905 instead: speeds combine in a way that is almost exactly adding when they are small, and that never gets past 1.

0clo1co0eq6fgm1rmm65mjetia.value: the ball's speed, on the train

iu0ru0poe1r8ib2dqgfd0oanh6.value: The dashed line is the speed of light. Newton's grey bar crosses it whenever the two speeds add up to more than 1, and the program's orange bar never does.

26sp524hp8o0i5aultn58uni4b.value: Try two small speeds, like 0.05 and 0.05. Newton says 0.1 and the program says 0.0995: almost the same. That is why Newton's rule works so well for everything slower than a space probe.

893ugt4gu00im9ld00p40hn8m7.value: How the program gets its answer

jk8okp3njk4bi5r9id4kvtp0be.value: The program doesn't contain any formula for adding speeds. It treats "start moving at this speed" as a kind of turn, a turn in space and time together, which physicists call a boost.

6lanl9u599907rcr9uth69i6ah.value: Ordinary turns are easy to combine: turning by 30° and then by 40° is a turn by 70°. Boosts combine the same way, except that what adds up is not the speed but a number called its rapidity. For slow things, rapidity and speed are nearly the same number. For fast things they part ways: the speed is tanh of the rapidity, a curve that rises steeply at first and then flattens out just under 1.

8b0e5jdhguluovk7v61fin1jbj.value: So the program turns each speed into a boost, does one boost after the other (in the algebra, it multiplies them), and reads off how fast the ball ends up going. The rapidities have added, and the speed for that added rapidity is on the flat part of the curve, below 1. Stack as many boosts as you like and it stays below 1.

7sahk455o8at8th7268u406t8c.value: rapidity of the ball, on the train

0otpssjbp7ke5f5a868a1q90i9.value: the speed the program read off its product

36o00ia2r68fvo9p1ah6a5k5n3.value: Across is rapidity, up is speed. The orange dot is the two rapidities added, and its height is the ball's speed for the platform. The last two rows agree: the curve and the program's product are two ways to the same answer.

ammqopm3s78i9i0kkp2dt34ngo.value: Part 2: a charge pushed by electric and magnetic fields

6f2beu8dbhrcd4trqbtjiienuo.value: The second question is about something pushed rather than thrown: an electric charge, say an electron, in a place with an electric field and a magnetic field. Electric motors, old television tubes and particle accelerators are all built on this.

vrlsnfp46cemppjabmi8smqej0.value: An electric field pushes a charge along the field, the way gravity pulls a dropped ball down. On its own, it would speed the charge up in a straight line.

6gmduvj6bmm5754c1arropl6nt.value: A magnetic field pushes only a charge that is moving, and always sideways to the way it moves. On its own, it bends a moving charge round in circles without speeding it up or slowing it down.

5q9sb607kssvtag2jjl3dici51.value: Here the electric field (E) points up the screen, and the magnetic field (B) points straight out of the screen, towards you. The charge starts at rest. E gets it moving upwards. As soon as it moves, B pushes it sideways, which bends it round to the right and then back down until it stops, and then E starts it off again, a little further to the right. The path is a row of loops that drifts to the right.

aqv7s4d0ahr1rrld00mbsmls7p.value: Newton's laws, with the push Lorentz worked out for a moving charge, give exactly that row of loops, drifting at a speed of E divided by B. But that means when E is as strong as B, Newton's charge drifts at the speed of light, and when E is stronger, faster than light.

uon5raa56ptkg0bh1k9t1quuht.value: magnetic field B (out of the screen)

n600h1gtsrliqar66aqn230s9m.value: Both start at rest at the black dot and run for the same 24 units of time. The dotted circle, when it fits, is how far light gets in that time: nothing should leave it. The picture zooms to fit both paths.

q6gq99h1d1q0ms4aks8pkfd6kt.value: With no electric field nothing gets the charge moving, so it stays where it started.

ta7enql9giculg1va5ifei2bt6.value: B is stronger than E, so both charges loop and drift to the right. While B is much stronger than E the two paths lie on top of each other, because the charge never goes fast. Move E closer to B and they come apart. The program's charge gets close to light speed, its clock runs slow, and its loops stretch out, until at about E = 0.9 it doesn't finish even one loop in the time shown. Newton's loops are always the same kind of loop, only bigger.

2r1r134vgtnsuuanjv9kskp0hs.value: E is at least as strong as B. Newton's charge still loops, but drifts at E/B, at or past the speed of light, so it leaves the dotted circle. The program's charge stops looping and runs away to the right, faster and faster, but never past light: it stays inside the circle.

3naovgulo0hugh0c88pq7cmfs9.value: How the program gets its answer

vjsa193etus3tpvd8st2qhvu57.value: The same idea as in Part 1. In the spacetime algebra, the electric and magnetic fields together are a single object, and that object turns the charge's motion a little at every moment. When B is stronger than E the turn is an ordinary rotation, so the charge goes round in loops. When E is stronger the turn is a boost, so the charge keeps speeding up, the way Part 1's boosts did, and like them it never reaches the speed of light. When the two are equal it is a turn in between.

9n0pr1rnc7a9nmsju41ojg0684.value: Each step, the program makes the small turn for that moment and applies it to the charge's motion. It takes a step of the platform's time, and the charge's own clock runs a little slow when it moves fast, which the program accounts for too.

hnnte1aqjbc27erej6fve78qia.value: One more thing: the field depends on who is looking

dtc2p08i12tklfu4bg1q1gl6mn.value: Someone running past the charge sees a different mix of electric and magnetic field. Move fast enough to the right through the field above, and to you some of the magnetic field turns into electric field. The program works that out with the same boosts as Part 1, turning the field object rather than a speed.

lfqk6pcmqqcqgqeu9thlcem87s.value: E up, for someone standing still

asodedkts4ate1eak60bqvv7en.value: B out of the screen, standing still

eavpu8vd813icr9spanlsq7cqo.value: B out of the screen, for you

d9q695gjf55hc2r34gcqrg8klk.value: E² − B², standing still and for you

9ikmq70f33p2ihctkjqaceoip7.value: E and B change, but E² − B² comes out the same for everyone. So whether the charge loops (B stronger) or runs away (E stronger) doesn't depend on who is watching, which is just as well.

eub9n7h1cbv6pfhlccik3gt9di.value: The algebra is Cl(1, 3), the spacetime algebra: four directions γ₀ (time) and γ₁, γ₂, γ₃ (space), with γ₀² = 1 and γₖ² = −1. A multivector has 16 parts. The speed of light is 1.

muq6fu22mpnf2g05fg4ta2dkk8.value: Part 1. The boost by speed β along x is the rotor R = e^(φ/2 σ₁), with σ₁ = γ₁γ₀ and rapidity φ = artanh β. Since σ₁² = +1, the exponential gives cosh and sinh: a boost is a hyperbolic rotation. Two boosts multiply to R₂R₁ = e^((φ₁ + φ₂)/2 σ₁), and the ball's four-velocity is R₂R₁ γ₀ (R₂R₁)~, whose γ₁ part over its γ₀ part is tanh(φ₁ + φ₂) = (β₁ + β₂)/(1 + β₁β₂).

mlabufimmkk75b8l26ktjfp85q.value: Part 2. The field is one bivector, F = E + I B, with I = γ₀γ₁γ₂γ₃. The charge's four-velocity obeys du/dτ = F · u, and over a step dτ it turns as u → R u R̃ with R = e^(dτ F/2) (Hestenes). F² = E² − B² + 2I E·B: when F² < 0 the step rotor is a rotation, when F² > 0 a boost, and when F² = 0 it is 1 + dτF/2. Here E and B are at right angles, so F² is a number and clifford exp makes the rotor in closed form, with cos and sin or cosh and sinh. For fields at other angles the prelude has clifford exp by series.

ef8iq1qv74o1vdf08k1t9kprj2.value: One more thing. A moving observer sees F′ = R̃ F R. A sandwich by a rotor can't change F², so E² − B² and E·B are the same for every observer.
